summary.text: Assuming a bound \(B\), set \(k=B+2\) and \(n=10^k-1\); the final step shows \(a(n)\) has the same digit sum as a positive multiple \(M\) of \(n\), so that digit sum is at most \(B\). Folding the digits of \(M\) modulo \(k\) yields a positive \(V=C(10^k-1)\) with \(1\le C<10^k\) and digit sum at most \(B\), whereas \(V=(C-1)10^k+(10^k-C)\) has digit sum exactly \(9k>B\), a contradiction.

full_proof.text:
Let \(Z(m)\) denote the natural number obtained from the ordinary decimal expansion of \(m\) by deleting every digit equal to zero. For example, \(Z(105020)=152\). Let \(R_n\) be the set of values reachable after \(n\) steps. Thus
\[
R_0=\{1\},
\]
and, recursively,
\[
R_{n+1}=\bigcup_{y\in R_n}\{(n+1)y,\; Z((n+1)y)\}.
\]
Every \(R_n\) is a nonempty finite set, and the sequence in question is
\[
a(n)=\min R_n.
\]
We prove that this sequence is not bounded.

Write \(s(m)\) for the sum of the decimal digits of \(m\). We will need several elementary properties of \(s\).

First,
\[
s(Z(m))=s(m),
\]
because deleting zero digits does not change the sum of the digits. Also
\[
s(m)\le m
\]
for every natural number \(m\), and
\[
s(m)=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad m=0.
\]
For completeness, these follow directly by induction on the number of decimal digits. If \(m>0\), write \(m=10q+r\), where \(0\le r<10\). Then
\[
s(m)=r+s(q).
\]
Inductively \(s(q)\le q\), and hence
\[
s(m)\le r+q\le r+10q=m.
\]
The same recurrence shows that a positive integer has positive digit sum. The identity \(s(Z(m))=s(m)\) follows by expressing \(m\) as its list of decimal digits: filtering out the zero entries leaves the sum of that list unchanged.

It follows in particular that every reachable value is positive. Indeed, this is clear at stage zero. If \(y>0\), then \((n+1)y>0\). Its digit sum is positive, and deleting its zero digits preserves that digit sum, so \(Z((n+1)y)>0\) as well. Thus
\[
y\in R_n\quad\Longrightarrow\quad y\ge 1.
\]

We next establish the digit-folding fact used in the proof. Fix an integer \(k>0\), and let
\[
q=10^k-1.
\]
Suppose the decimal expansion of a natural number \(M\), written from least significant digit upward, is
\[
M=\sum_{j\ge0}d_j10^j,
\]
where only finitely many \(d_j\) are nonzero and \(0\le d_j<10\). Define its cyclic \(k\)-folding by
\[
V=\sum_{j\ge0}d_j10^{j\bmod k}.
\]
This construction has four important properties.

First,
\[
V\equiv M\pmod q.
\]
Indeed, \(10^k\equiv1\pmod{10^k-1}\). If \(j=uk+r\), with \(0\le r<k\), then
\[
10^j=(10^k)^u10^r\equiv10^r=10^{j\bmod k}\pmod q.
\]
Multiplying by \(d_j\) and summing gives the congruence.

Second,
\[
V\le s(M)10^{k-1}.
\]
Every exponent \(j\bmod k\) is at most \(k-1\), so
\[
d_j10^{j\bmod k}\le d_j10^{k-1}.
\]
Summing over \(j\) gives the claimed bound because \(\sum_jd_j=s(M)\).

Third,
\[
s(V)\le s(M).
\]
One way to see this carefully is to use the elementary inequality
\[
s(X+10^i)\le s(X)+1.
\]
Adding \(10^i\) either increases the digit in position \(i\) by one, or creates a string of carries; carries can only decrease the resulting digit sum relative to an increase of one. Repeating this inequality gives
\[
s(X+c10^i)\le s(X)+c
\]
for every natural number \(c\). Starting from zero and adding the terms \(d_j10^{j\bmod k}\) one at a time therefore yields
\[
s(V)\le\sum_jd_j=s(M).
\]

Fourth, if \(M>0\), then \(V>0\). A positive \(M\) has at least one positive digit \(d_j\), and the corresponding summand \(d_j10^{j\bmod k}\) is positive.

We also need a decimal-complement identity. If \(0\le X<10^k\), then
\[
s(X)+s(10^k-1-X)=9k. \tag{1}
\]
To understand this, regard \(X\) as a string of exactly \(k\) decimal digits, permitting leading zeros. Since \(10^k-1\) is the string of \(k\) nines, subtraction from it requires no borrowing: every digit \(d\) of \(X\) is replaced by \(9-d\). Each corresponding pair of digits therefore has sum \(9\), proving (1). Equivalently, this identity follows by induction on \(k\), splitting off the highest digit of \(X\).

Another elementary estimate that will be used is
\[
B<10^{B+2}-1 \tag{2}
\]
for every natural number \(B\). This can be proved by induction. For \(B=0\), it says \(0<99\). If it holds for \(B\), then \(B+1\) is still less than \(10^{B+3}-1=10\cdot10^{B+2}-1\); indeed, the induction hypothesis gives \(B+1\le10^{B+2}-1\), while \(10^{B+2}-1<10\cdot10^{B+2}-1\). Notice also that \(10^{B+2}\ge100\).

We now derive the contradiction. Suppose, contrary to the claim, that there is a natural number \(B\) such that
\[
a(m)\le B
\]
for every \(m\). Set
\[
k=B+2,
\qquad
n=10^k-1.
\]
Then \(k>0\), \(n>0\), and by the assumed bound the least reachable value
\[
x=a(n)
\]
satisfies
\[
x\le B. \tag{3}
\]
Because \(x\in R_n\), examine the final, \(n\)-th, transition in a path reaching \(x\). There is some \(y\in R_{n-1}\) such that either
\[
x=ny
\]
or
\[
x=Z(ny).
\]
As shown above, every reachable value is positive, so \(y\ge1\). Put
\[
M=ny=(10^k-1)y.
\]
Thus \(M>0\), and the two alternatives for the last step are simply
\[
x=M\quad\text{or}\quad x=Z(M).
\]
In either case,
\[
s(x)=s(M), \tag{4}
\]
because this is immediate in the first case and follows from invariance of digit sum under zero deletion in the second. Combining (3), (4), and \(s(x)\le x\), we obtain
\[
s(M)=s(x)\le x\le B. \tag{5}
\]

Apply the cyclic \(k\)-folding construction to the decimal digits of \(M\), and call the resulting number \(V\). Since \(M=(10^k-1)y\), we have
\[
M\equiv0\pmod{10^k-1}.
\]
The folding congruence therefore gives
\[
V\equiv M\equiv0\pmod{10^k-1}.
\]
Moreover, \(M>0\), so \(V>0\). Consequently there is a positive integer \(C\) such that
\[
V=C(10^k-1). \tag{6}
\]
The folding bounds and (5) give
\[
V\le s(M)10^{k-1}\le B10^{k-1}, \tag{7}
\]
and
\[
s(V)\le s(M)\le B. \tag{8}
\]

We claim that
\[
C<10^k. \tag{9}
\]
If instead \(C\ge10^k\), then (6) would imply
\[
V\ge10^k(10^k-1).
\]
On the other hand, because \(k=B+2\), estimate (2) says
\[
B<10^k-1.
\]
Hence (7) gives
\[
V\le B10^{k-1}<(10^k-1)10^{k-1}< (10^k-1)10^k,
\]
contradicting the preceding lower bound. This proves (9).

Now use the special decimal form forced by (6). Since \(C>0\) and \(C<10^k\), ordinary arithmetic gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
V
 &=C(10^k-1)\\
 &=C10^k-C\\
 &=(C-1)10^k+(10^k-C). \tag{10}
\end{aligned}
\]
The second summand satisfies
\[
0<10^k-C<10^k.
\]
Thus (10) is a concatenation of the decimal expansion of \(C-1\) with a lower block of exactly \(k\) digit positions (again allowing leading zeros in that lower block). Therefore digit sums add across the two blocks:
\[
s(V)=s(C-1)+s(10^k-C). \tag{11}
\]
But
\[
10^k-C=10^k-1-(C-1),
\]
and (9) implies \(0\le C-1<10^k\). Applying the complement identity (1) with \(X=C-1\) gives
\[
s(C-1)+s(10^k-C)=9k.
\]
Together with (11), this yields
\[
s(V)=9k. \tag{12}
\]

Finally, (8) and (12) imply
\[
9k\le B.
\]
Yet \(k=B+2\), so
\[
9k=9(B+2)>B,
\]
a contradiction.

Therefore no natural number \(B\) can satisfy \(a(n)\le B\) for every \(n\). In other words, the sequence of minimum values obtainable by successive multiplication and optional deletion of zero digits is unbounded, disproving the boundedness conjecture.
